chapters.category: Ethiopic textual tradition • Modern English research translation
chapters.title: Chapter 74 — The Lunar Course and the 364-Day Year
chapters.sourceNote: Translated afresh into clear modern English from the earliest complete primary-language text responsibly available for this chapter. No extant Aramaic wording has been identified for the Astronomical Book, while the limited Greek fragments do not preserve this chapter in full. The complete Ethiopic (Geʽez) text in August Dillmann's 1851 critical edition, Liber Henoch Aethiopice, is the translation base for all seventeen verses: Uriel's record of the moon's waxing and portals, the relation between lunar and solar counts, and the stated totals for three-, five- and eight-year cycles. The numerical statements and ancient calendar model are translated as given rather than adjusted to a later astronomical system; no bracketed explanatory addition from a later translation is inserted into the Scripture text. No unattested wording was supplied, and no modern English translation was used as the translation base.

verses.text: I saw another course and command for the moon: according to that command it completes its monthly course.
verses.study: The lunar month is governed by an assigned course. Repetition becomes faithful fulfillment rather than mere recurrence.
crossReferences: Genesis 1:14 — the lights mark months and seasons
Psalm 104:19 — the moon is appointed for seasons

verses.text: Uriel, the holy angel who guides them all, showed me all these things and their positions. I wrote down their positions just as he showed me, their months as they are, and the appearance of their light until fifteen days were completed.
verses.study: Enoch writes what Uriel shows, limiting the record to received observation. The fifteen-day waxing interval is documented rather than embellished.
crossReferences: Habakkuk 2:2 — a vision is written for clear witness
Revelation 1:19 — the seer records what has been shown

verses.text: By single seventh parts the moon completes all its light in the east, and by single seventh parts it completes all its darkness in the west.
verses.study: Waxing and waning are described through matching portions. Light and darkness advance within one measured cycle.
crossReferences: Ecclesiastes 3:1 — every change has an appointed time
Daniel 2:21 — God governs times and seasons

verses.text: In certain months it changes its setting, and in certain months it follows its own course.
verses.study: Variation belongs inside the lunar law. Ordered creation can include differing monthly paths.
crossReferences: 1 Corinthians 15:41 — heavenly bodies possess differing glory
Psalm 148:6 — the lights keep the decree established for them

verses.text: In two months the moon sets with the sun, through the two middle portals, the third and the fourth portals.
verses.study: The middle portals mark months of shared setting. The vision relates lunar timing to the sun's portal course.
crossReferences: Genesis 1:16 — greater and lesser lights share the ordered heavens
Jeremiah 31:35 — sun and moon follow the Lord's ordinances

verses.text: It goes out for seven days, turns and returns through the portal from which the sun rises, and completes all its light. It withdraws from the sun and on the eighth day enters the sixth portal from which the sun goes out.
verses.study: Seven days of movement lead to a turn, fullness and a new portal on the eighth. The moon's separation from the sun is measured by stages.
crossReferences: Genesis 2:2–3 — seven days form a completed created pattern
Sirach 43:6–8 — the moon's phases mark appointed times

verses.text: When the sun goes out from the fourth portal, the moon goes out for seven days until it goes out from the fifth. It turns back again for seven days to the fourth portal and completes all its light; then it withdraws and enters the first portal in eight days.
verses.study: The moon moves among portals with a patterned seven-day return and eighth-day entry. Fullness is a station within continuing movement.
crossReferences: Psalm 19:6 — the heavenly course extends across the sky
Ecclesiastes 1:5 — the lights return along recurring paths

verses.text: Again it returns in seven days to the fourth portal from which the sun goes out.
verses.study: The return to the fourth portal ties the lunar course back to the solar point of reference.
crossReferences: Psalm 104:19 — sun and moon know their appointed times
Job 38:33 — ordinances govern the heavens

verses.text: In this way I saw their positions, how the moons rise and the sun sets in those days.
verses.study: Enoch summarizes the vision as observed positions. The plural cycles of the moon are read alongside the sun's setting.
crossReferences: Psalm 8:3 — the moon and stars invite attentive contemplation
Psalm 19:1–2 — heaven's ordered witness speaks day after day

verses.text: When five years are added together, the sun has an excess of thirty days. All the days belonging to one full year within those five years total 364 days.
verses.study: The five-year comparison exposes a thirty-day difference while reaffirming the solar year's stated total.
crossReferences: Genesis 1:14 — years are reckoned through the lights
Psalm 90:12 — numbering days serves wisdom

verses.text: The excess of the sun and the stars is six days each year; over five years the six days become thirty. The moon therefore falls thirty days behind the sun and the stars.
verses.study: Annual differences accumulate across the cycle. Careful counting makes divergence visible rather than confusing the separate courses.
crossReferences: 1 Chronicles 12:32 — understanding times supports wise action
Daniel 7:25 — times and their alteration carry moral significance

verses.text: The sun and the stars bring in all the years exactly. They neither advance nor delay their position by one day forever, but complete the years in exact righteousness in 364 days.
verses.study: Accuracy is called righteousness because the lights remain true to their commission. Cosmic regularity becomes an image of dependable obedience.
crossReferences: Psalm 119:89–91 — creation stands by God's ordinances
Jeremiah 33:20 — day and night keep their established covenant

verses.text: In three years there are 1,092 days, and in five years 1,820 days; therefore in eight years there are 2,912 days.
verses.study: The totals extend the 364-day reckoning across larger cycles. The arithmetic serves transparent preservation of the calendar.
crossReferences: Deuteronomy 4:6 — careful observance displays wisdom
Luke 14:28 — faithful planning includes counting the total

verses.text: For the moon alone, its days in three years total 1,062 days; in five years it falls behind by fifty days.
verses.study: The lunar count is distinguished from the 364-day solar count. The difference is reported rather than concealed.
crossReferences: Genesis 1:14 — multiple lights contribute to timekeeping
Ecclesiastes 3:1 — distinct seasons retain distinct measures

verses.text: In five years there are 1,770 lunar days; therefore the moon's days in eight years total 2,832 days.
verses.study: The combined lunar totals continue the chapter's comparative reckoning. Precision allows different cycles to be held together without merging them.
crossReferences: Proverbs 27:23 — careful knowledge requires attentive accounting
1 Corinthians 14:40 — ordered practice reflects clarity

verses.text: For over eight years it falls behind by eighty days; all the days by which it falls behind in eight years are eighty.
verses.study: The repeated total emphasizes the accumulated divergence between lunar and solar reckonings.
crossReferences: Psalm 90:12 — counted days train understanding
Ecclesiastes 7:25 — wisdom searches out the sum of a matter

verses.text: The year is completed exactly according to their positions and the positions of the sun, which rises from the portals through which it rises and sets for thirty days.
verses.study: The chapter closes by returning calculations to visible stations. The complete year rests on the coordinated positions and portal courses already described.
crossReferences: Psalm 19:4–6 — the sun completes its heavenly circuit
Psalm 148:3–6 — sun, moon and stars keep the Creator's decree

explanation.heading: Chapter teaching and context
paragraphs: Chapter 74 continues Uriel's instruction by recording the moon's portal movements and its increase toward fullness. Enoch repeatedly identifies writing as preservation of what was shown.
The lunar course is coordinated with the sun yet remains distinct. Seven-day movements, eighth-day entries and changing portals describe an ordered relationship rather than identical paths.
The second half compares the 364-day solar year with lunar totals across three, five and eight years. Differences accumulate predictably and are stated openly through the chapter's arithmetic.
Righteousness here describes exact faithfulness to an appointed station. The sun, moon and stars do not advance or delay their commission, making cosmic order a witness to dependable obedience.

crossReferences: Genesis 1:14–18 — lights appointed to measure time
Psalm 19:1–6 — heaven's ordered course declares glory
Psalm 104:19 — moon and sun know appointed times
Psalm 119:89–91 — creation continues by divine ordinance
Jeremiah 31:35–36 — fixed orders govern the lights
Sirach 43:6–8 — lunar change marks months
